resident.chief_complaint: Squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: The patient is a 49-year-old male. Symptoms started approximately three months prior to the initial visit with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling sensations in both upper and lower extremities. He reported no difficulty in walking. He demonstrated Lhermitte's sign when extending the neck abruptly. He denied any sensory and motor change. A diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine had been made before hospital admission.
resident.physical_exam: The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination. Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Motor power and reflexes are not documented.
key_positive_signs: Lhermitte's sign on abrupt neck extension
resident.past_history: Diagnosis of ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) of the cervical spine was made before hospital admission. No other past medical history is documented.
resident.public_message: This 49-year-old male presented with a squeezing feeling at the midsection and tingling in both upper and lower extremities, symptoms beginning about three months before presentation. He had no difficulty walking. The patient denied any sensory and motor change on physical examination; however, Lhermitte's sign was elicited on abrupt neck extension. Imaging showed OPLL from C2 to C5 with atlas hypoplasia, spinal canal stenosis from C1 to C5 with cord compression at the atlas ring and an intramedullary high signal intensity area. Preoperative JOA score was 15 points.

imaging.public_message: I have not seen the films and am reporting only the case record's imaging description: OPLL was described from C2 through C5, with spinal canal stenosis from C1 through C5 and especially marked canal narrowing with cord compression at the atlas ring. An intramedullary high-signal area was reported. The record does not specify compression direction or a graded stenosis severity. These findings correlate well with the reported Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord, most likely at C1-2 (atlas ring) given the marked canal stenosis and cord compression. Lhermitte sign and bilateral upper and lower extremity tingling with truncal squeezing are consistent with cervical myelopathy involving the dorsal columns and possibly spinothalamic tracts. Motor and reflex findings are not documented, so precise long-tract involvement is inferred.

red_flags.finding: Motor power and reflexes are not documented; sensory examination reportedly normal despite subjective tingling.
red_flags.rationale: This is an examination gap, not evidence of an alternative cause. Lhermitte sign is a positive finding and imaging shows cord compression, so the absence of documented motor/reflex changes does not undermine the myelopathic localization.

red_flags.finding: Marked canal narrowing and cord compression at the atlas ring due to atlas hypoplasia, distinct from the OPLL at C2-C5.
red_flags.rationale: If surgical decompression is planned primarily for OPLL at C2-C5, the upper cervical compression at C1-2 may require additional or different surgical consideration. The cord compression at the atlas ring is part of the same cervical myelopathy but could change the operative approach.

neurology.public_message: Findings localize to the cervical spinal cord, most likely C1-2, with Lhermitte sign and bilateral sensory symptoms. No symptom-imaging mismatch.

physiatrist_opening.public_message: I acknowledge the imaging demonstrates significant stenosis and cord signal change; however, the patient currently presents with mild symptoms (JOA 15, no motor or gait deficits documented, only subjective tingling and Lhermitte sign). A structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management—cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, avoidance of high-risk maneuvers, and close neurological surveillance—is a reasonable first step. Surgical decompression is indicated only if there is objective neurological deterioration (new motor weakness, gait decline, sphincter involvement) or worsening T2 signal on follow-up MRI. The success rate of observation and conservative therapy in mild myelopathy without obvious motor deficit is approximately 40%, and a trial can be undertaken safely with frequent reassessment.

vice_opinions.assessment: This 49-year-old male has a clinical myelopathy (JOA 15, Lhermitte sign, bilateral sensory symptoms) with imaging showing severe cervical stenosis from OPLL C2-C5, atlas hypoplasia, cord compression at the C1 ring, and intramedullary T2 signal. Although motor and reflex findings are not documented and the current deficit appears mild, the combination of multilevel OPLL, C1 stenosis, and cord signal change raises the risk of neurologic deterioration and catastrophic injury from minor trauma. In my view, the imaging findings are too significant to comfortably recommend prolonged observation without a complete neurologic assessment and additional imaging. The atlas ring compression must be surgically addressed if decompression is undertaken; a routine subaxial procedure alone would be inadequate. Before finalizing a surgical plan, I would obtain full motor/reflex/gait documentation, dynamic radiographs, a detailed CT of the OPLL and atlas, and an airway evaluation.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical decompression including C1 laminectomy and C1-C5 laminoplasty or laminectomy, with fusion if instability or kyphosis is present. This addresses the atlas ring and subaxial stenosis in a single procedure.

Anterior decompression (corpectomy or floating OPLL resection) for subaxial compression if ventral pathology dominates and lordosis is maintained. This does not address the C1 hypoplasia and carries higher risk for dural ossification/CSF leak.
Combined anterior-posterior decompression if both ventral OPLL and dorsal/atlas stenosis require direct decompression and posterior alone is judged insufficient.
Structured conservative management with close neurologic and MRI surveillance, accepting the risk of progression, and proceeding to surgery only with objective deterioration.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical decompression including C1 laminectomy with laminoplasty/laminectomy C1-C5 and fusion if instability or kyphosis, after completion of missing neurologic exam and dynamic/CT imaging. The posterior approach addresses the atlas hypoplasia and provides adequate indirect decompression for OPLL in a lordotic spine, which is the most defensible initial surgical strategy.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the rehabilitation physician's recommendation for a 3-6 month conservative trial in this specific case. OPLL with C1 cord compression and intramedullary signal change carries a higher risk of rapid deterioration and trauma-related injury than typical mild spondylotic myelopathy; a delay may forfeit a window for safer elective decompression.

The JOA score of 15 is unreliable without documented motor, reflex, and gait findings. The patient may have subtle myelopathy already; I would not label this as truly mild until the full exam is available.

The surgical plan must explicitly include decompression of the atlas ring. A subaxial-only procedure would leave the most severe stenosis untreated; this is a critical planning point that should not be overlooked.
deferred_questions_to_director: Given the high-risk imaging and mild documented symptoms, do you concur with proceeding to surgical decompression now rather than an initial conservative trial?
Should we request additional workup before finalizing the plan: dynamic flexion-extension films, CT for OPLL and atlas anatomy, complete neurologic exam, and anesthesia airway evaluation?
If surgery is chosen, do you favor posterior decompression alone versus combined anterior-posterior given the uncertainties about OPLL dominance and sagittal alignment?
vice_opinions.public_message: From a spine surgery perspective, the imaging is highly concerning: C1-C5 stenosis with OPLL, atlas hypoplasia, and cord signal change. Even with mild current symptoms, the risk of deterioration is significant. I favor surgical decompression after completing the missing neurologic and imaging data, and the procedure must include the C1 level. I have reservations about a prolonged conservative trial in this particular case.

vice_opinions.assessment: The imaging is highly concerning: multilevel OPLL, C1-C5 stenosis, atlas hypoplasia, cord compression at the C1 ring, and intramedullary T2 signal change. Although the current examination is reported as JOA 15 with only subjective sensory symptoms and Lhermitte sign, the documented motor, reflex, and gait findings are absent. This is a high-risk myelopathy profile. I agree with the Director that we must complete the missing workup before making a final recommendation. However, my surgical threshold is low: if CT and dynamic imaging confirm severe C1 stenosis or instability, or if the neurologic examination reveals myelopathic signs, surgical decompression including the C1 level is indicated. A conservative trial is only defensible if all data confirm truly mild, stable disease without dynamic risk, and even then it should have strict failure criteria and a short re-evaluation interval. I defer the final decision to the Director after the workup.
